Isometric Log-Ratio Transform

Source: R/log_ratio_transforms.r
ilr.Rd

Coordinates of each sample in an orthonormal basis of the Aitchison simplex: Egozcue et al.'s isometric log ratio (ilr). Euclidean distances between them are Aitchison distances, for any basis.

Usage

ilr(counts, basis = NULL, margin = 1L, pseudocount = NULL, cpus = n_cpus())

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of non-negative abundances (samples \(\times\) features), or any of the objects listed under Input Types. Counts, proportions, and the output of a zero replacement are all accepted: each sample's scale cancels out of the log ratios.

basis

The ilr basis, one of:

  • NULL (the default): the Helmert basis that scikit-bio's ilr() uses (built by Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization). Coordinate \(j\) is the balance of the first \(j\) features against feature \(j + 1\): row \(j\) has \(\frac{1}{j}\sqrt{j/(j+1)}\) in columns \(1, \dots, j\), \(-\sqrt{j/(j+1)}\) in column \(j + 1\), and zeros after.

  • A sequential binary partition (SBP): a \((D - 1) \times D\) matrix of 1, -1 and 0, one row per balance, 1 marking the features in its numerator and -1 those in its denominator. Each row's \(r\) entries of 1 become \(\sqrt{s / (r (r + s))}\) and its \(s\) entries of -1 become \(-\sqrt{r / (s (r + s))}\), as scikit-bio's sbp_basis(). Every row needs both signs, and the partition must be sequential (its balances orthogonal).

  • An orthonormal basis in clr coordinates: a numeric \((D - 1) \times D\) matrix with orthonormal rows that each sum to 0 (checked to \(10^{-6}\), as scikit-bio checks orthonormality).

A matrix has one row per coordinate and one column per feature (scikit-bio's orientation). Its columns are matched to the features by name when both have names, and by position otherwise. Its row names name the coordinates.

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

pseudocount

Added to every value before taking logs. NULL (the default) adds nothing when counts has no zeros, and otherwise uses half the smallest non-zero value, with a warning. See Pseudocount.

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

Value

A dense numeric matrix of the \(D - 1\) coordinates, in the orientation of counts: samples \(\times\) coordinates for margin = 1, coordinates \(\times\) samples for margin = 2 (and for a single sample given as a vector). Sample names are kept. Coordinates are named by rownames(basis), or ilr1, ilr2, .... Attributes:

  • method: 'ilr'.

  • basis: the \((D - 1) \times D\) basis used (an SBP converted to its basis), with its columns in the order of the features of counts, so that coords %*% basis gives back normalize(counts, 'clr') (for margin = 1). For the default basis of more than 1000 features, whose matrix would take more than 8 MB, it is the string 'helmert' instead.

  • pseudocount: the pseudocount used (0 for none).

Details

For a sample \(x\) with clr coordinates \(\mathrm{clr}(x) = \log(x + c) - \overline{\log(x + c)}\) (natural logs, \(c\) the pseudocount) and a basis \(\Psi\) with orthonormal rows, $$\mathrm{ilr}(x) = \mathrm{clr}(x)\,\Psi^T.$$ The default basis is applied by a running sum, in \(O(D)\) per sample, and other bases through their non-zero entries, so an SBP costs only its non-zeros.

Because the coordinates are orthonormal, euclidean(ilr(x)) is aitchison(x) (with the same pseudocount), whichever basis is used: for distances, use aitchison(). ilr() is for analyses of the coordinates themselves: regression, lda() or rda() without the clr's singular covariance, and balances that can be interpreted, from an SBP. The coordinates feed straight into pca(), rda(), lda(), envfit() and euclidean() with norm = 'none'.

ilr(x + c) here equals scikit-bio's ilr(x + c) (and ilr(x + c, sbp_basis(sbp))) to rounding.

Same names in other packages: compositions::ilr() and robCompositions::pivotCoord() compute ilr coordinates with other default bases (compositions::ilr()'s default is this one with the opposite sign). Whichever package was attached last masks the other's ilr(); write ecodive::ilr() to be sure.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

Pseudocount

Logs of zero are undefined, so zeros need replacing first. The pseudocount is added to every value (not only to zeros), as in normalize(norm = 'clr'). With pseudocount = NULL (the default), no pseudocount is used when counts has no zeros; otherwise half the smallest non-zero value is, with a warning. To avoid a pseudocount, replace the zeros first with replace_zeros(): its result has none.

The choice of pseudocount is not neutral: it can distort the results, especially for sparse tables. See aitchison() for references.

Machine learning

Log-ratio transforms (clr, rclr, alr, ilr, PhILR) serve interpretation and compositional geometry; don't expect them to improve prediction. With random forests predicting 65 metadata variables in four datasets, Yerke et al. (2024) found that alr, clr and ilr (PhILR) "performed generally slightly worse or only as well as compositionally naïve transformations", and relative abundances did best, by a small margin. Compare with norm = 'percent' (see normalize()) before choosing a log-ratio predictor table.

References

Egozcue, J. J., Pawlowsky-Glahn, V., Mateu-Figueras, G., & Barceló-Vidal, C. (2003). Isometric logratio transformations for compositional data analysis. Mathematical Geology, 35, 279–300.

Egozcue, J. J., & Pawlowsky-Glahn, V. (2005). Groups of parts and their balances in compositional data analysis. Mathematical Geology, 37, 795–828.

Yerke, A., Fry Brumit, D., & Fodor, A. A. (2024). Proportion-based normalizations outperform compositional data transformations in machine learning applications. Microbiome, 12, 45. doi:10.1186/s40168-023-01747-z

See also

alr(), normalize() ('clr' and 'rclr'), aitchison()

Examples

    x <- ilr(ex_counts, pseudocount = 1)
    dim(x)
#> [1] 4 5

    # Euclidean distances on ilr coordinates are Aitchison distances
    all.equal(
      as.vector(euclidean(x, norm = 'none')),
      as.vector(aitchison(ex_counts, pseudocount = 1)) )
#> [1] TRUE

    # Balances from a sequential binary partition of 4 features
    sbp <- rbind(
      c(1,  1, -1, -1),
      c(1, -1,  0,  0),
      c(0,  0,  1, -1) )
    ilr(ex_counts[, 1:4], basis = sbp, pseudocount = 1)[1:3, ]
#>              ilr1     ilr2      ilr3
#> Saliva  0.4969327 2.824989 -3.675893
#> Gums    1.9045923 3.583367 -3.165955
#> Nose   -1.5385559 1.440293  3.616140
